## Food and wine excursions: wine, coffee and local cuisine in Latin America

Culinary travel introduces a region through its produce and the people who grow, prepare and serve it. Some excursions take you to wineries, others show how coffee beans are processed, offer chocolate tastings or invite you to prepare a traditional dish alongside a local expert. These experiences offer more than flavor: behind every product lies the history of a town, family or farming region.

Our catalog features stand-alone food and wine excursions in several Latin American countries. They differ in format, duration and included services. A tasting during a visit to a single farm and a full wine-touring day with lunch are different programs; compare precisely what each one includes before choosing.

## Wine excursions in Argentina

### Mendoza: from one winery to a full day

[Mendoza](/argentina/place/mendoza/) is one of Argentina's leading wine regions. Vineyards stretch against the backdrop of the Andes, and visitors can see the facilities used to make and age wine. Programs may include walks among the vines, introductions to grape varieties and tastings. The region's best-known grape is Malbec.

For an introduction, choose a [Mendoza winery excursion](/argentina/mendoza/mendoza-wineries-wine-tasting/). If you want to devote a whole day to wine, we offer a [tour of 3 wineries in Luján de Cuyo with lunch](/argentina/mendoza/argentina-lujan-three-wineries-lunch/). Its current description confirms visits and tastings at three wineries, with lunch at the third. The exact wineries are agreed upon when booking, so the program should not be associated with particular brands in advance.

Another option is a [wine tasting in the Uco Valley](/argentina/uco-valley/uco-valley-winery-tasting/). This separate district south of Mendoza is known for its mountain scenery and vineyards. Choosing between Luján de Cuyo and Uco involves different locations, transfers and numbers of wineries, not merely different grape varieties in the glass.

### Wine and the culture of Buenos Aires

Travelers staying in the capital do not have to go to the mountains to explore the country's food culture. A [Buenos Aires food tour](/argentina/buenos-aires/buenos-aires-food-tour/) introduces the city through its dishes and local habits. It is a convenient option for trips already filled with museums, city neighborhoods and other excursions, where a separate multi-day wine itinerary is not planned.

## Wineries in Chile and Uruguay

In Chile, you can choose a [Maipo Valley wine tour](/chile/maipo-valley/maipo-valley-wine-tour/) or a [private wine day in central Chile](/chile/millahue-valley/chile-private-wine-day-millahue/). The second excursion describes private tastings, walks among the vineyards and culinary experiences. The specific wineries and whether a separate dinner is included must be confirmed for the chosen program: these details significantly affect both the day's length and its final cost.

For a different combination of wine and urban culture, consider a [Montevideo tour with a winery visit](/uruguay/montevideo/montevideo-city-winery-tour/). The current eight-hour program combines sightseeing in the capital with a tasting and lunch. Uruguay is particularly associated with the Tannat grape, although the winery determines the exact wines served during a tasting.

| Region | Main format |
|---|---|
| Mendoza and Uco | Vineyards in the Andes |
| Central Chile | Private wine experiences |
| Montevideo | City sightseeing and tasting |

This comparison helps distinguish a production-site excursion from a city walk where a glass of wine is merely an addition.

## Coffee and chocolate in Colombia

In Colombia's coffee-growing region, travelers learn how coffee cherries are cultivated, how the beans are processed and how coffee is brewed in different ways. A [coffee farm near Pereira](/colombia/pereira/pereira-coffee-farm-tour/) offers a five-hour experience that includes an explanation of flavor profiles and a tasting. Transfers and an English-speaking guide are confirmed in the description; lunch is listed separately from the included services.

Another option is [El Ocaso farm near Salento](/colombia/salento/el-ocaso-coffee-farm-tour/). You can consider it as part of a journey through the coffee region, comparing its location, production demonstration and tasting experience.

For travelers interested in a different product, there is a [chocolate farm excursion in Pereira](/colombia/pereira/pereira-chocolate-farm-tour/). Understanding cacao involves processes different from coffee roasting. Compare these two products for their content, rather than treating them both simply as “farm tastings.”

## Cooking classes and dinners

In [Rio de Janeiro](/brazil/place/rio-de-janeiro/), you can choose a [caipirinha-making class](/brazil/rio-de-janeiro/caipirinha-making-class/) or a [Brazilian churrasco cooking class](/brazil/rio-de-janeiro/brazilian-churrasco-cooking-class/). The first focuses on preparing a drink; the second introduces a meat-grilling tradition. Participation, duration and tasting experiences differ.

On the Brazilian coast, try a [Paraty trip featuring waterfalls and cachaça](/brazil/paraty/paraty-waterfalls-cachaca-jeep/). This combines a nature excursion with a culinary stop. It suits travelers who want variety, but it is not equivalent to a lengthy cooking course.

Another option is an [evening dinner show in the Iguazu area](/brazil/foz-do-iguacu/rafain-dinner-show/). Visitors interested in regional culture can also enjoy a [folklore dinner in Lima](/peru/lima/lima-folklore-dinner-show/). In both cases, check the menu and the performance's starting time beforehand.

## How to choose a food and wine excursion

First decide what matters most: tasting products, seeing how they are made or learning to prepare dishes yourself. The guiding language and group size also matter. Winery tasting selections vary, while farm excursions can differ in how much walking is involved on the property.

When comparing tours, pay attention to four details: how many stops are confirmed, whether tastings are included, whether lunch is provided and whether a long transfer is required. Any of these can substantially change the experience.

Winemaking is seasonal: Mendoza's grape harvest usually occurs in late Southern Hemisphere summer and early autumn. Wineries may welcome visitors outside the harvest season, but participation in production work should never be promised without confirmation.

## Food and wine excursions on multi-country journeys

A journey through Argentina, Chile and Uruguay offers a chance to explore differences between their wine regions. Adding Colombia gives it a very different emphasis: coffee, cacao and tropical agricultural traditions. Our [food and wine travel page](/interests/food-and-wine/) brings together related regions and itineraries; this catalog specifically lists stand-alone excursions.

For journeys across several countries, see the [multi-country catalog](/multi-country/). Compare the actual stops in each itinerary: merely mentioning a wine-producing country does not guarantee a winery visit.

## Frequently asked questions about food and wine excursions

### What is the difference between a tasting and a complete winery visit?

A tasting focuses on sampling and learning about drinks. A complete winery visit may also include vineyards, production facilities and an explanation of winemaking. The exact content depends on the program.

### Is lunch included in wine excursions?

Sometimes. For example, lunch is confirmed on the [3-winery Luján de Cuyo tour](/argentina/mendoza/argentina-lujan-three-wineries-lunch/). It may be absent from other excursions.

### Are there excursions without alcohol?

Yes. Coffee and chocolate farms, food-preparation classes and other culinary activities introduce local cuisine without wine tastings.

### Which region should I choose for my first wine journey?

Mendoza and the Uco Valley offer an introduction to Argentine wine against the backdrop of the Andes. Chile and Uruguay have their own formats. Your choice depends on the geography and duration of your entire trip.

## Food and wine tours in Latin America: where to begin

**The most useful question to ask before choosing a culinary journey is what you want to learn beyond the taste of a drink or dish.** A wine trip may focus on grape varieties, how wineries operate and conversations with winemakers. A coffee itinerary reveals how beans are grown, harvested and processed. A city food tour introduces markets, neighborhood cuisines, recipes and everyday life.

All three approaches can be combined with a standard sightseeing itinerary. But if a particular product interests you, it is better to devote full days to it than to rely on a chance tasting between transfers. Our [food and wine tour page](/interests/food-and-wine/tours/) features {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}}. These include dedicated itineraries and combined journeys where culinary experiences occupy only part of the program.

Choose according to the content of each day: is a specific winery or farm named, is there a production tour, and are a tasting, lunch or cooking class included? The word “gastronomic” in a tour title does not explain what is covered by the price or how much time is allocated to the visit.

## Argentina: Malbec, Mendoza and wine valleys at the foot of the Andes

[Mendoza](/argentina/place/mendoza/) is one of the leading destinations for exploring Argentine wine. Its vineyards grow in an arid climate near the Andes. Vineyard elevation, differences between daytime and nighttime temperatures, soils, irrigation and the work of the winemaker all matter. Malbec is among the region's recognizable grapes, but a trip need not focus on one variety alone: comparing estates reveals differences in winemaking approaches and the character of local wines.

Within the region, distinguish between [Luján de Cuyo](/argentina/place/lujan-de-cuyo/), Maipú and the Uco Valley. Each area has its own location and mix of traditional and modern estates. If wine is your central interest, plan visits to neighboring wineries on the same day rather than spending most of the time on the road. In the [Uco Valley](/argentina/place/uco-valley/), vineyards lie against a mountain backdrop, and production tours can be combined with lunch and walks among the vines. Visits to specific wineries need to be booked in advance.

On the [7-day culinary tour of Argentina](/argentina/tour/argentina-food-fine-living/), [Buenos Aires](/argentina/place/buenos-aires/) and gaucho traditions are combined with several days in Mendoza. The program includes visits to wineries and an introduction to production. It is an example of a journey in which gastronomy is central, while city experiences complement the trip.

For a comparison of wines across countries, there is a [9-day Argentina and Chile itinerary](/multi-country/tour/chile-argentina-mendoza-wine-9-days/) covering [Buenos Aires](/argentina/place/buenos-aires/), wineries in the [Uco Valley](/argentina/place/uco-valley/), [Santiago](/chile/place/santiago-de-chile/) and Chile's Concha y Toro. This format suits travelers wishing to compare two winemaking traditions, though flights or long transfers between regions must be considered. Other options appear in our [Argentina food and wine tour collection](/interests/food-and-wine/tours/argentina/).

## Chile and Uruguay: how their wine itineraries differ

Chile is best explored valley by valley. Near Santiago lies the [Maipo Valley](/chile/place/maipo-valley/), known for red wines. Closer to the Pacific is [Casablanca](/chile/place/casablanca-valley/), where white varieties have a prominent role. The [Colchagua](/chile/place/colchagua-valley/) and [Cachapoal](/chile/place/cachapoal-valley/) valleys are also among the country's major wine destinations. Their differences reflect climate, proximity to the ocean and producers' approaches. Rather than booking a generic “Chilean vineyard tour,” it is better to select two or three specific wineries in one region.

[Concha y Toro](/chile/place/concha-y-toro/) near [Santiago](/chile/place/santiago-de-chile/) introduces visitors to a historic estate, vineyards and the story of the Casillero del Diablo brand. The aforementioned Mendoza–Santiago journey explicitly includes this visit. When choosing [Chile food and wine tours](/interests/food-and-wine/tours/chile/) independently, check whether winery stops are included in the main itinerary or offered as optional excursions.

Uruguay offers another wine tradition. One of its best-known grapes is Tannat, strongly associated with local cuisine and meat dishes. But Uruguayan wine is about more than one variety: wineries differ by region, soil, style and setting. You can combine visits to [Montevideo](/uruguay/place/montevideo/), colonial towns and the history of winemaking.

[Spinoglio Winery](/uruguay/place/spinoglio-winery/) north of [Montevideo](/uruguay/place/montevideo/) preserves a historic nineteenth-century cellar. The [Uruguay: Wine and Old Believer Traditions tour](/uruguay/tour/uruguay-wine-old-believer-traditions/) combines a visit to the estate with Montevideo, [San Javier](/uruguay/place/san-javier/), [Fray Bentos](/uruguay/place/fray-bentos/) and [Colonia del Sacramento](/uruguay/place/colonia-del-sacramento/). It suits travelers interested equally in wine culture and the country's history. Another place to discover local winemaking is [Garzón Winery](/uruguay/place/garzon-winery/), where tastings are paired with seasonal cuisine.

When deciding between Argentina, Chile and Uruguay, consider your priority: several days in a major wine region, comparisons between producers in different countries, or a relaxed combination of wine and city walks. Comparing the actual itinerary days is more useful than counting the countries mentioned in the title.

## Coffee tours: Colombia, Brazil and Costa Rica

On a [coffee journey](/interests/coffee-tours/), flavor comes alive through cultivation and processing. Even coffees from the same country can taste very different depending on plantation elevation, cherry ripeness, processing, roasting and brewing methods. This is why seeing the entire journey of coffee on a farm is particularly rewarding: plant growth, harvesting, pulping, drying, roasting and tasting.

Colombia's coffee-growing region covers the mountain slopes of the western and central Andes. Its cultural landscape was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2011. This recognition is not about coffee's advertising reputation, but the agricultural landscape itself: small plantations, mountain settlements, architecture and the way of life of coffee-growing families.

On the [Colombia Coffee tour](/colombia/tour/colombia-coffee/), the sightseeing itinerary begins in [Bogotá](/colombia/place/bogota/) before continuing to [Pereira](/colombia/place/pereira/), a coffee farm, [Salento](/colombia/place/salento/) and the [Cocora Valley](/colombia/place/cocora-valley/). Other journeys may include [El Ocaso Coffee Farm](/colombia/place/el-ocaso-coffee-farm/) near Salento, where visitors learn about growing, processing and preparing coffee, or [Hacienda Coloma](/colombia/place/hacienda-coloma/) near Bogotá. These are actual places featured by Ada Tours, but their inclusion in a specific itinerary must be checked rather than assumed from the country name.

Brazil's [Coffee Valley in Rio de Janeiro State](/brazil/place/coffee-valley-rio-de-janeiro/) tells a different story. Old fazendas and manor houses associated with the nineteenth-century coffee boom survive here. Plantation history includes enslaved labor, an important subject when visiting historic estates. The [8-day coffee plantations and Iguazu tour](/brazil/tour/brazil-coffee-plantations-iguazu-8-days/) combines Rio, the falls and a dedicated day at an old coffee fazenda. It is more a journey into coffee history and the country as a whole than a program devoted entirely to modern bean-processing methods.

In Costa Rica, a relevant site is [Doka Estate](/costa-rica/place/doka-estate/) near [Poás Volcano](/costa-rica/place/poas-volcano/). Visiting it provides an introduction to rural Costa Rica and stages of coffee processing. To include this stop, choose a program that explicitly visits the plantation or arrange an extra excursion. Compare options among [Costa Rica coffee and culinary tours](/interests/food-and-wine/tours/costa-rica/).

For coffee lovers, the choice between countries can be straightforward: [Colombia](/colombia/) introduces modern mountain farms, [Brazil](/brazil/) around Rio explores plantation history, and [Costa Rica](/costa-rica/) combines a rural setting and production cycle near nature routes. You can compare these approaches in a long journey, but extensive transfers for every individual cup of coffee are unlikely to be worthwhile.

## Cuisine in Mexico and Peru: from the market to traditional recipes

Gastronomy goes far beyond wine and coffee. Traditional Mexican cuisine is built around corn, beans, chili peppers and diverse regional techniques. In 2010, UNESCO included traditional Mexican cuisine, with particular attention to the practices of Michoacán, on its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. The inscription recognizes a whole system of growing produce, preparing corn, making dishes and passing on knowledge, rather than one famous recipe.

A journey through [Mexico City](/mexico/place/mexico-city-and-teotihuacan/) with culinary stops showcases the diversity of taquerías, markets and neighborhood eateries. The published [Mexico gourmet tour](/mexico/tour/mexico-gourmet-discovery-2024/) includes walks through [Coyoacán](/mexico/place/coyoacan/) and an introduction to tacos and mezcal. The same itinerary also features [Teotihuacán](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/), [Chichén Itzá](/mexico/place/chichen-itza/) and the Yucatán, combining food with archaeology and relaxation. Travelers interested exclusively in cooking activities may prefer a more focused route; the number of culinary meals and excursions on a combined journey is limited by its program.

Peru is especially interesting for the diversity of produce from its coast, Andes and Amazon. One of its best-known dishes is ceviche, fish marinated in citrus juice and chili. In 2023, UNESCO recognized the practices of preparing and consuming Peruvian ceviche as intangible cultural heritage. The recognition concerns local recipes, the knowledge of fishers and cooks and community life, not any one restaurant.

In [Lima](/peru/place/lima/), city walks can be paired with a market or a Peruvian restaurant to explore the cuisine. The current [Peru journey featuring the Hiram Bingham train](/peru/tour/peru-belmond-hiram-bingham-machu-picchu/) lists gourmet dinners in Lima, [Cusco](/peru/place/cusco/) and during the rail journey. This illustrates how cuisine can complement a cultural itinerary; ceviche or a particular cooking class is not automatically included.

Learn more about combining food and historical monuments in our [cultural and historical travel section](/interests/culture-and-history/). The [Mexico food and wine tour collection](/interests/food-and-wine/tours/mexico/) also lets you compare trips in which food and local traditions occupy different proportions of the journey.

## Which to choose: a winery, farm, market or cooking lesson?

| Format | What travelers experience |
|---|---|
| Winery | Production, grape varieties, tasting |
| Coffee farm | Growing and processing coffee beans |
| City market | Local produce and everyday cuisine |
| Cooking class | Hands-on preparation of a dish |
| Gourmet dinner | Culinary techniques and flavor pairings |
| Historic fazenda | Agricultural history |

**One format rarely replaces another.** A wine-bar tasting helps compare varieties, but does not show vineyards or the production cycle. A coffee-farm excursion explains where the beans come from, yet may not include a detailed class on preparing the drink. A market visit introduces the city and its products; a cooking workshop provides practical experience. If you want some of everything, limit the number of essential activities and leave free time between them.

There is also a distinction between culinary stops included in a package and independent opportunities along the way. On each [food and wine tour page](/interests/food-and-wine/tours/), look beyond the final list of cities: check where a guide is provided, which estates are named, whether tastings and a set lunch are included, and which excursions cost extra.

## When to travel for wine, coffee and local cuisine

In southern South America, the grape harvest mainly falls in late local summer and early autumn. In [Mendoza](/argentina/place/mendoza/), harvest season usually runs from February to April, though timing varies by year, grape variety and vineyard. Winemaking activity is especially visible then, but wineries can also be visited in other seasons. Summer offers a view of ripening grapes; in winter, the emphasis may shift to cellars, production techniques and tastings.

In Chile, the calendar varies with the valley and climate: coastal [Casablanca](/chile/place/casablanca-valley/) and warmer inland regions have different agricultural cycles. In Uruguay, seasonal dishes and weather shape the atmosphere of a wine journey, although many estates welcome guests outside harvest time. In every case, confirm tour hours, booking requirements and available tasting formats with the chosen winery before visiting.

Coffee follows its own pattern: ripening and harvest depend on the region and altitude, and some locations have several harvest periods each year. Coffee tours can take place even when few ripe cherries remain on the bushes, with the visit focusing on processes, production, history and tasting. If seeing the harvest itself is important to you, check the season at the specific farm rather than relying on a country's general calendar.

City food walks are possible year-round. Local festivals, market hours and the seasonality of particular products tend to have a greater influence here. Transfers and weather deserve special attention when an itinerary crosses several climate zones.

## Planning a journey without unnecessary transfers

First choose your main theme and allocate several full days to it. For wine, that may mean a wine region and neighboring city; for coffee, a farm, nearby settlement and natural attractions; for cuisine, a city, its markets and historic neighborhoods. Only then add a second country or another kind of vacation.

The more stops you include, the more important it becomes to count flights, hotel changes and hours on the road rather than kilometers on a map. For example, it makes more sense to visit wineries in the [Uco Valley](/argentina/place/uco-valley/) on a series of outings from [Mendoza](/argentina/place/mendoza/) than to combine them with [Buenos Aires](/argentina/place/buenos-aires/) attractions in one day. A Colombian coffee-region trip requires travel between [Bogotá](/colombia/place/bogota/) and [Pereira](/colombia/place/pereira/). Visiting Brazil's historic [Coffee Valley](/brazil/place/coffee-valley-rio-de-janeiro/) from [Rio](/brazil/place/rio-de-janeiro/) also takes a substantial part of the day.

Before confirming a program, check transportation after wine tastings: a driver or organized transfer is needed if participants plan to consume alcohol. Inform the organizer in advance about food allergies, vegetarian diets and other restrictions. If you travel with children or have no interest in alcohol, choose programs where food experiences are not limited to wine tasting. Farms, markets and cooking classes offer different experiences, but their individual participation rules must still be confirmed.

## Frequently asked questions about food and wine tours

### Which country should I choose for my first wine journey?

[Argentina](/argentina/), especially Mendoza, suits travelers who want to spend several days in one wine region. [Chile](/chile/) makes it easy to compare valleys and producers. [Uruguay](/uruguay/) combines smaller estates, Tannat, local cuisine and historic towns. Choose by what the wineries offer and the time you have, not just the reputation of the wines.

### How does a coffee tour differ from an ordinary plantation excursion?

On a [coffee tour](/interests/coffee-tours/), growing, processing and the history of coffee form a substantial part of the itinerary. On a general tour, a plantation may be one stop among cities and natural sites. For greater depth, look for programs with time for a farm visit, explanations of processing methods and a tasting.

### Can wine, cuisine and cultural sightseeing be combined?

Yes. Wine and history work well together in [Buenos Aires](/argentina/place/buenos-aires/) and [Mendoza](/argentina/place/mendoza/); local food and archaeology in [Mexico](/mexico/); and coffee and city life in [Colombia](/colombia/). For example, the [Argentina and Chile tour including Mendoza](/multi-country/tour/chile-argentina-mendoza-wine-9-days/) combines wineries, city excursions and an introduction to gaucho traditions.

### Are alcoholic tastings required?

No. Culinary travel extends beyond wine tastings: you can choose coffee, agriculture, markets, local cooking and hands-on classes. At a winery, specific non-alcoholic alternatives depend on the program and the venue's rules; agree on them before booking.

### Are restaurant dinners, cooking classes and winery visits included in the tour price?

It depends on the chosen itinerary. Some tours specifically list wineries and dinners as included; others offer culinary stops as add-ons. Read the day-by-day itinerary and the “Included” and “Not included” sections. Neither the tour title nor a “food and wine” label establishes which services are paid for.

### When is the best time to plan a wine tour during harvest?

For [Mendoza](/argentina/place/mendoza/), February–April is a useful guide, though actual harvest dates vary. Wineries are open for visits in other months too. If you want to watch grape harvesting or participate in a special activity, choose dates confirmed by the specific winery's program; the season alone does not guarantee access to fieldwork.

### How much time should you allow for a culinary journey?

For one wine region, you could allocate several days, leaving a day for the city and transfers. Combining a capital, a distant coffee region and nearby natural attractions requires a longer itinerary. Our existing programs provide different options; the choice primarily depends on how many complete days you want to spend on the culinary experiences themselves.

## Food and wine in Latin America: flavorful places to explore

A culinary journey becomes especially rewarding when food, wine or coffee is a meaningful part of the itinerary. [Mendoza](/argentina/place/mendoza/) in Argentina introduces vineyards near the Andes, the [Colchagua Valley](/chile/place/colchagua-valley/) in Chile offers a different wine region, and [Pereira](/colombia/place/pereira/) in Colombia is a gateway to coffee estates.

We have gathered places connected with [food and wine journeys](/interests/food-and-wine/). The program matters when choosing: a winery tasting, a cooking workshop and an ordinary lunch on a city tour are different experiences. The mere presence of restaurants in a city does not make a tour a culinary journey.

## Argentina: Mendoza, Luján de Cuyo and the Uco Valley

[Mendoza](/argentina/place/mendoza/) is the main base for exploring western Argentina's wine regions. [Luján de Cuyo](/argentina/place/lujan-de-cuyo/) is home to wineries associated with several well-known red grape varieties. The [Uco Valley](/argentina/place/uco-valley/) offers a different landscape, with vineyards against the backdrop of the Andes.

Trips through these regions require winery visits to be arranged in advance, as each estate has its own entry rules, tasting schedules and capacity for groups. Several tastings in succession also raise transportation considerations: arrange a separate driver for travel after sampling wine.

In northwestern Argentina, [Cafayate](/argentina/place/cafayate/) is known for its high-altitude wine region, with a climate and location different from Mendoza. It is not a quick additional tasting stop near the capital; reaching it requires a separate route through Salta.

For concrete itineraries, see [Argentina wine and food tours](/interests/food-and-wine/tours/argentina/).

## Chile: valleys with different climates

The [Maipo Valley](/chile/place/maipo-valley/) and [Concha y Toro Winery](/chile/place/concha-y-toro/) are often part of wine journeys near Santiago. But a visit to a specific estate requires an agreed time, a selected tasting format and transportation.

The [Colchagua Valley](/chile/place/colchagua-valley/), [Casablanca Valley](/chile/place/casablanca-valley/) and [Millahue Valley](/chile/place/millahue-valley/) differ in their distance from the capital, climate and selection of wineries. If wine production is your main interest, compare these regions according to a definite visit program, not a promotional photograph of a vineyard.

One busy day in a nearby valley and several days with overnight stays in wine regions are substantially different travel experiences.

## Colombia: coffee farms and mountain towns

Colombia's Coffee Cultural Landscape is inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List. It is a network of rural and urban areas where coffee-growing history is connected with local families' lives, architecture and the way the crop is processed.

[Pereira](/colombia/place/pereira/), [Salento](/colombia/place/salento/), [Filandia](/colombia/place/filandia/) and [Armenia](/colombia/place/armenia/) let travelers explore different parts of the coffee region. When choosing an estate, it is especially interesting to see the complete sequence from the plant and harvesting cherries to processing and tasting, provided that all those stages are part of the current visit.

Among the individual sites in our catalog are [Hacienda Venecia](/colombia/place/hacienda-venecia/) and [El Ocaso Coffee Farm](/colombia/place/el-ocaso-coffee-farm/). Entry arrangements and tasting opportunities at each property should be confirmed separately.

## Brazil: historic coffee estates and traditional cuisine

In Brazil, culinary itineraries can focus on coffee, regional cuisine and tasting experiences. [São Paulo](/brazil/place/sao-paulo/) connects contemporary urban life with the state's coffee history, while some routes visit historic rural estates.

There is a [private Brazil coffee tour](/brazil/tour/brazil-private-coffee-tour/) and other programs in which coffee forms a substantial theme. For a culinary journey, check whether there will be an actual encounter with production or whether the itinerary simply travels through a former coffee-growing area.

## Uruguay: wineries near Montevideo

Uruguayan wineries are found in [Canelones](/uruguay/place/canelones/) and neighboring areas. Individual sites in our catalog include [Bouza](/uruguay/place/bouza-winery/), [Garzón](/uruguay/place/garzon-winery/) and [Spinoglio](/uruguay/place/spinoglio-winery/).

These are good examples of why studying the map matters: wineries can lie in different parts of the country, and visits to three estates may not fit conveniently into one day. Check logistics, tasting types and meals in the program.

## Mexico and Central America: local cuisine and production

[Oaxaca](/mexico/place/oaxaca/) in Mexico is known for its markets, regional dishes and craft traditions. Culinary experiences here can be combined with historical sights and the culture of the region.

[Matagalpa](/nicaragua/place/matagalpa/) in Nicaragua, [Boquete](/panama/place/boquete/) in Panama and [Huehuetenango](/guatemala/place/huehuetenango/) in Guatemala are associated with rural and coffee-growing areas. To learn about production firsthand, arrange in advance which farms can be visited and whether access is possible.

## Choosing a food and wine destination

| Interest | Where to look |
|---|---|
| Wine | Argentina, Chile, Uruguay |
| Coffee | Colombia, Brazil |
| Local cuisine | Mexico, Peru |
| Production | Wineries, farms |

Restaurants, wine tastings and chef-led classes may be separate programs. In each case, duration, estate operations and the services included matter. Do not assume that everyone visiting a wine region will automatically tour a winery.

## Frequently asked questions about food and wine destinations

### Which countries are best for wine?

That depends on your preferred wines and travel logistics. Mendoza in Argentina, Chile's wine valleys and Uruguay's wineries offer different experiences, so choose based on specific tastings and the time available.

### Can coffee experiences be combined with nature excursions?

Yes. Some coffee-growing regions are close to natural areas, but plantation visits and nature trips should be planned as separate activities.

### Does every tour passing through Mendoza include a tasting?

No. Only selected programs explicitly include a winery visit or tasting; the rest of the itinerary does not establish that such a service is provided.

## What to combine with food and wine tours in Latin America

**The most natural pairings are gastronomy with culture, nature, coffee farms and beach holidays.** Each appeals to a different interest. Some travelers want to understand a wine region's history, while others dream of seeing a volcano or spending several days on the coast after touring a coffee farm.

Food and wine can be the main reason for travel or one element of another trip. In the first case, allow time for several estates, tastings and introductions to local dishes. In the second, choose a few substantial stops along the way. Compare all available programs in the [food and wine tour catalog](/interests/food-and-wine/tours/).

| Combination | Best for |
|---|---|
| [Culture and history](/interests/culture-and-history/) | Wineries, cities, traditions |
| [Coffee tours](/interests/coffee-tours/) | Plantations, farms, tastings |
| [Nature](/interests/nature/) | Wine or coffee plus landscapes |
| [Wildlife and safari](/interests/wildlife/) | Coffee and wildlife watching |
| [Beach holidays](/interests/beach-holidays/) | Excursions and days by the sea |
| [Events and festivals](/interests/events-and-festivals/) | Urban celebrations and cuisine |

An itinerary tagged with both themes indicates they are compatible, but actual visits still need to be checked against the program. A winery visit and a free evening at a restaurant, for example, offer very different levels of culinary immersion.

## Wine and culture: Argentina and Chile

Wine journeys combine well with city excursions. A region's history becomes easier to appreciate after exploring its neighborhoods, markets and traditions. This is particularly true in [Mendoza](/argentina/place/mendoza/), where viticulture exists alongside the history of migration, urban architecture and life at the foot of the Andes. Argentine tourism authorities highlight wineries, vineyards and traditional cuisine as distinct reasons to visit the region.

On the [9-day Argentina and Chile tour](/multi-country/tour/chile-argentina-mendoza-wine-9-days/), the cultural section begins in [Buenos Aires](/argentina/place/buenos-aires/), with a city tour, gaucho traditions and tango. The itinerary then visits wineries in the [Uco Valley](/argentina/place/uco-valley/), continues to Santiago and includes [Concha y Toro](/chile/place/concha-y-toro/). This is an example of wine and culture playing substantial roles in both countries rather than appearing as incidental stops.

Another format is [Argentina for Lovers of Wine, Cuisine and the Good Life](/argentina/tour/argentina-food-fine-living/). The capital's historic neighborhoods, tango and gaucho traditions are paired with Mendoza. The program also describes optional activities: when comparing itineraries, distinguish what is included in the basic package from what is selected separately.

If you primarily want to understand a country through its cities and people, start with [cultural and historical itineraries](/interests/culture-and-history/tours/). If you are ready to set aside dedicated days for wine, compare [Argentina food and wine programs](/interests/food-and-wine/tours/argentina/) by wineries visited and time between excursions.

## Food and coffee: two related but different goals

[Coffee tours](/interests/coffee-tours/) now form a separate travel category in our collection. This makes it easier to choose journeys devoted specifically to coffee production: cultivation, harvesting, bean processing and tastings. The broader [food and wine section](/interests/food-and-wine/) also includes wine, urban cuisines, markets and other agricultural products. The themes may overlap on the same trip.

On the [private Brazil coffee tour](/brazil/tour/brazil-private-coffee-tour/), a visit to the historic [Coffee Valley in Rio de Janeiro State](/brazil/place/coffee-valley-rio-de-janeiro/) is combined with sightseeing in Rio and a journey to [Iguazu Falls](/brazil/place/foz-do-iguacu/). This suits travelers interested in the history of coffee estates who also want to see Brazil's famous sights. For a more specialized choice, see the [Brazil coffee-tour catalog](/interests/coffee-tours/tours/brazil/).

In Colombia, a coffee farm can be combined with historic cities and beaches. For example, the [Colombia VIP: Bogotá, Coffee Region, Cartagena and Barú tour](/colombia/tour/colombia-vip-coffee-cartagena-baru-10-days/) includes Bogotá, a visit to the coffee region, [Cartagena](/colombia/place/cartagena/) and a finale on Barú. However, being included in a VIP selection does not itself imply additional services; the program description determines exactly what is offered.

Colombia's coffee region also has independent cultural significance. UNESCO inscribed the Coffee Cultural Landscape of Colombia on its World Heritage List in 2011. It includes agricultural landscapes and settlements shaped by growing coffee on the Andean slopes. A farm visit can therefore be an introduction to architecture and the lives of local communities as well. Relevant options are listed among [coffee tours in Colombia](/interests/coffee-tours/tours/colombia/).

## Wine or coffee plus nature: what should come first?

If vineyards and natural scenery interest you, compare itineraries by distance and the order of regions. A tasting and a short mountain trip can be combined within one area; glaciers, tropical forests and waterfalls demand a longer journey.

The [Buenos Aires, Mendoza, El Calafate and Iguazu tour](/argentina/tour/argentina-buenos-aires-mendoza-el-calafate-iguazu/) illustrates a wide-ranging option. Following city tours and Mendoza wineries, the route continues to [Perito Moreno Glacier](/argentina/place/perito-moreno-glacier/) and then to Iguazu. There are many memorable experiences, but travel between the regions takes up a substantial part of the trip. Travelers prioritizing nature should also compare [Argentina nature tours](/interests/nature/tours/argentina/).

Costa Rica offers an example that is more compact in theme, although transfers are still involved. On the [Costa Rica Treasures tour](/costa-rica/tour/costa-rica-treasures/), a visit to [Doka Coffee Estate](/costa-rica/place/doka-estate/) is paired with [Poás Volcano](/costa-rica/place/poas-volcano/), waterfalls and natural parks. Coffee occupies a substantial part of one day; the other days explore the country's landscapes and animals. Compare similar trips among [Costa Rica coffee tours](/interests/coffee-tours/tours/costa-rica/) and [Costa Rica nature tours](/interests/nature/tours/costa-rica/). There is also a separate [Costa Rica wildlife collection](/interests/wildlife/tours/costa-rica/).

If extended wildlife watching is your priority, choose routes with several days devoted to parks and animals. If your main goal is tasting and learning about production, ensure that nature outings leave sufficient time for the estates.

## Local cuisine, the ocean and major festivals

Culinary experiences fit especially naturally into a visit to Brazil's Atlantic coast. Historic [Paraty](/brazil/place/paraty/) is known for local traditions and cachaça production. UNESCO inscribed Paraty and [Ilha Grande](/brazil/place/ilha-grande/) together as a World Heritage Site for their combination of culture and biodiversity. Urban life, cuisine, forests and the sea come together in this one area.

The [Flavors of Brazil: Rio Carnival, Paraty and Ilha Grande tour](/brazil/tour/carnival-flavors-rio-paraty-ilha-grande/) begins with Carnival activities in Rio. In Paraty, the program includes a distillery and an introduction to cassava-flour production, followed by a seaside stay. This brings together several themes: [events and festivals](/interests/events-and-festivals/), [culture](/interests/culture-and-history/) and [beach holidays](/interests/beach-holidays/). If Carnival is your main reason for going, the dates of festival events become your priority; check the details on the chosen tour page.

Another way to finish a culinary journey by the sea is the previously mentioned [Colombia trip with the coffee region and Barú Island](/colombia/tour/colombia-vip-coffee-cartagena-baru-10-days/). Here, days on the Caribbean coast follow city visits and coffee-production experiences. For more options, explore [Colombia food and wine tours](/interests/food-and-wine/tours/colombia/) and [Colombia beach itineraries](/interests/beach-holidays/tours/colombia/).

## Fishing and cuisine: when the catch becomes part of the experience

For travelers interested in cooking, restaurants are only part of the story; seeing how local ingredients are harvested and prepared can be equally rewarding. The [one-day Ushuaia to Puerto Almanza trip](/argentina/tour/ushuaia-fishing/) includes a boat outing with fishers and a king crab lunch. Travelers see how coastal fishing connects with regional cuisine. Nevertheless, this is primarily a [fishing program](/interests/fishing/), not a wine tour or conventional culinary itinerary.

This combination suits those who care about the process. If sampling several wines or taking a cooking class is more important, a separate fishing trip might use too much of your time. Compare the day's purpose and included services before adding it to your route.

## Choosing a combination without overloading the trip

First identify the **main activity** that brings you to Latin America. For wine enthusiasts, that might mean several wineries and an unhurried exploration of one region. For history lovers, it could be city walks with one substantial culinary stop. Priorities will differ for family trips, nature journeys or beach holidays.

Then examine the program day by day. Separate included visits from optional tastings and free evenings. Check transfer times, how long you will spend at estates, event dates and the conditions of your itinerary. Interesting activities should remain complete experiences rather than turning into a string of short stops.

Finally, compare neighboring catalogs by their actual programs: [food and wine](/interests/food-and-wine/tours/), [coffee journeys](/interests/coffee-tours/tours/), [cultural and historical tours](/interests/culture-and-history/tours/), [nature journeys](/interests/nature/tours/) and [wildlife-watching trips](/interests/wildlife/tours/). The same tour may appear in several collections because it combines activities. Your final choice depends on its route and what each day contains.

## Frequently asked questions about combining food and wine with other interests

### Can wine tastings and historical excursions be combined?

Yes. On the [Argentina and Chile itinerary including Mendoza](/multi-country/tour/chile-argentina-mendoza-wine-9-days/), winery visits are paired with Buenos Aires, gaucho culture and Santiago. Check the list of wineries and day-by-day order if you want wine to be the main focus.

### How does a coffee tour differ from a food and wine tour?

A [coffee tour](/interests/coffee-tours/) focuses on estates, cultivation and bean processing. [Food and wine journeys](/interests/food-and-wine/) encompass a wider range of activities: winemaking, markets, regional cuisine and cooking programs. Both themes may feature on the same itinerary.

### Where can I combine a coffee plantation with volcanoes and natural parks?

On the [Costa Rica Treasures tour](/costa-rica/tour/costa-rica-treasures/), a visit to Doka Estate precedes the Poás Volcano trip and other nature excursions. For a specialized interest in coffee, there are separate [Costa Rica coffee itineraries](/interests/coffee-tours/tours/costa-rica/).

### Can I add a beach stay to a coffee-region journey?

Yes, for example on the [Colombia itinerary with the coffee region, Cartagena and Barú](/colombia/tour/colombia-vip-coffee-cartagena-baru-10-days/). The coffee-region visit comes before seaside relaxation. The number of free beach days depends on the particular program.

### Are all tastings and cooking activities included in the price of a combined tour?

Not necessarily. Some programs include them, while others offer a tasting or additional activity as an option. Check the day description, “Included” and “Not included” sections and conditions of the specific [tour](/interests/food-and-wine/tours/).

### What should I choose with limited time: a wine region or several countries?

For a deeper introduction to wine, it is usually easier to stay in one region: fewer transfers and more time at the wineries. A journey across several countries makes sense when you want to compare cultural traditions and see more places. Base the decision on the actual duration and number of full excursion days.

## Which food and wine tours in Argentina should you choose?

**If wine is your main reason for traveling, choose an itinerary with full days at Mendoza's wineries.** Cafayate is the destination for high-altitude wines and northwestern cuisine; the area around Buenos Aires offers asado and gaucho traditions. In Tierra del Fuego, the culinary focus is quite different: seafood and king crab.

Our catalog includes {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}}. They share an interest in food and wine but serve different purposes. Some are designed around tastings from the outset; in others, cuisine complements cities, nature or a journey through several countries. For multi-country tours, check where the wine activities actually take place: an itinerary may include Argentina while the tasting occurs in Chile.

| Your interest | Where to start |
|---|---|
| Malbec and wineries | [Mendoza](/argentina/place/mendoza/), [Uco Valley](/argentina/place/uco-valley/) |
| Northwestern wine | [Cafayate](/argentina/place/cafayate/), [Salta](/argentina/place/salta/) |
| Asado and gauchos | [Buenos Aires](/argentina/place/buenos-aires/), [Santa Susana Ranch](/argentina/place/santa-susana-ranch/) |
| Crab and coastal cuisine | [Ushuaia](/argentina/place/ushuaia/), [Puerto Almanza](/argentina/place/puerto-almanza/) |

The priority here is to compare **actual itineraries**, not to compile an encyclopedia of Argentine cuisine. Geography, climate and general logistics are covered in more detail in the [Argentina guide](/argentina/). To compare the country with Chile, Brazil and other destinations, see our [food and wine travel section](/interests/food-and-wine/).

## Mendoza: when wine becomes the heart of the trip

[Mendoza](/argentina/place/mendoza/) is a convenient base for discovering wine regions near the Andes. In the [Uco Valley](/argentina/place/uco-valley/), travelers see vineyards set against mountains, learn about production and sample local wines. [Luján de Cuyo](/argentina/place/lujan-de-cuyo/) is another important wine region, particularly for Malbec. Estates offer different formats: an introduction to production, a professional tasting, or a lunch with food and wine pairings. One does not automatically include another.

On the [9-day Argentina and Chile wine tour](/multi-country/tour/chile-argentina-mendoza-wine-9-days/), day 4 is devoted entirely to the Uco Valley: visits to **3 wineries** with a specialist guide, introductions to winemaking, tastings and lunch at one of the estates. The next day can be spent relaxing in Mendoza or **optionally** enjoying a tasting in Luján de Cuyo. The route then continues to Santiago and the Pacific coast; the visit to a Chilean winery takes place in another country. This trip suits travelers interested in the differences between wine regions as well as the two capitals.

The [7-day Argentina for Lovers of Wine, Cuisine and the Good Life tour](/argentina/tour/argentina-food-fine-living/) follows a different structure. It begins in Buenos Aires with a gaucho experience, then flies to Mendoza. Day 5 includes a **group wine tour with an English-speaking guide**, visits to 2–3 wineries and an introduction to tasting principles. An additional wine outing is possible on day 6, but it is an option rather than a required second tasting day. This is a good introduction to wine culture without sacrificing the city experience.

If you want to pair one busy wine day with major natural landmarks, compare the [tour through Mendoza, El Calafate and Iguazu](/argentina/tour/argentina-buenos-aires-mendoza-el-calafate-iguazu/). Day 5 features **3 Uco Valley wineries, a tasting and lunch**. The itinerary then continues to Perito Moreno Glacier and the waterfalls. This is a useful compromise for a first trip to Argentina if vineyards matter to you but you do not intend to spend most of your vacation visiting them.

**What to compare:** check the number of mandatory winery visits, whether tastings are included, the guide's language and lunch arrangements. Look separately at optional outings and free days. These details distinguish the three programs significantly, even though all include Mendoza.

## Salta and Cafayate: high-altitude vineyards and northern cuisine

In Argentina's northwest, a wine journey looks quite different. [Cafayate](/argentina/place/cafayate/) lies in the Calchaquí Valleys and is known for high-altitude winemaking, particularly the aromatic white Torrontés grape. Roads wind between dry mountains and multicolored slopes. The culinary experience can include traditional northwestern Argentine dishes such as empanadas, tamales, humita and locro. In [Salta](/argentina/place/salta/), visitors can taste local food at peñas, venues featuring live folk music in the evenings.

The [5-day Amazing Salta tour](/argentina/tour/amazing-salta/) begins with a trip to Cafayate. According to the published itinerary, travelers visit a winery, learn about grape cultivation and wine production, then explore the wine museum. The overnight stay is at a wine hotel. In the following days, the itinerary shifts to Los Cardones National Park, Purmamarca, Humahuaca Gorge and the Salinas Grandes salt flats. **Lunch on Cafayate's main square is paid separately**; it is not automatically included in the winery visit.

The longer [12-day Buenos Aires, Salta and Iguazu itinerary](/multi-country/tour/buenos-aires-salta-iguazu/) also includes a day in Cafayate: a winery estate, an introduction to winemaking, a wine museum and accommodation at a wine hotel. But the tour extends beyond wine: neighborhoods of the capital and tango, historic sites and mountainous landscapes of the northwest, followed by Iguazu Falls. If you want several consecutive tasting days, one winery visit in Cafayate may not be enough. If you prefer to pair wine with a broader exploration of the northwest, this route makes sense.

Mendoza and Cafayate are **two different kinds of wine journey**. Mendoza has a wider choice of existing programs visiting multiple wineries; in the itineraries mentioned through Cafayate, wine is an important stop within a trip through mountains and historic places. Both regions can be combined in one journey, but flights, overland transfers and hotel nights must be planned separately.

## Buenos Aires: asado, ranches and dinner with tango

A culinary journey through Argentina does not have to begin in the vineyards. [Buenos Aires](/argentina/place/buenos-aires/) introduces travelers to asado, the tradition of cooking meat over fire, Argentine empanadas and restaurant cuisine. A visit to an estancia adds rural life, folklore and gaucho culture to the meal. This is a different format from tasting wine with a winemaker.

On the [7-day wine and cuisine tour](/argentina/tour/argentina-food-fine-living/), one day is devoted to an estancia, with gaucho demonstrations and a **traditional Argentine lunch**, before the program continues to Mendoza. It is a chance to compare two distinctive food experiences on one trip: the pampas and the vineyards.

The [6-day Argentina: Buenos Aires, Tigre and Gaucho Traditions program](/argentina/tour/argentina-experience-6-days/) is organized for a group. It includes dinner during a tango show, separate lunches on excursions and a traditional barbecue at [Santa Susana Ranch](/argentina/place/santa-susana-ranch/). However, most days are devoted to the city, the Paraná Delta and a trip to Uruguay, not independent cooking activities. The dining arrangements are specific to this group itinerary.

On the [9-day Argentina and Chile wine journey](/multi-country/tour/chile-argentina-mendoza-wine-9-days/), dinner and drinks are part of a tango evening in Buenos Aires. But that meal does not replace the wine-country program: the route later travels to the Uco Valley for tastings. Decide in advance what matters most: an evening in the city, a gaucho outing or an in-depth exploration of winemaking. You can choose a combination that gives each experience its own time.

## Ushuaia: king crab instead of a wine itinerary

Southern Argentina has its own culinary specialty. From [Ushuaia](/argentina/place/ushuaia/), travelers head to [Puerto Almanza](/argentina/place/puerto-almanza/), a fishing village on the Beagle Channel. Here you can try king crab, known locally as centolla. This Tierra del Fuego seafood tradition is very different from Andean wineries or asado on the pampas.

On the current [one-day crab-fishing program](/argentina/tour/ushuaia-fishing/), travelers drive from Ushuaia to Puerto Almanza, go out on a boat with local fishers for approximately **25 minutes**, and then have lunch at a fishing restaurant. Under the published conditions, lunch consists of **3 courses, a non-alcoholic drink and a glass of wine or craft beer**. Although primarily a fishing excursion, the local food experience is a significant part of the day.

When choosing this excursion, consider weather, water conditions and restrictions on harvesting seafood. The presence of centolla on a restaurant menu does not mean fishing trips operate on every date. If wine tastings are your principal aim, Ushuaia will not replace Mendoza; visitors come here for different food and scenery.

**If your main goal is wine tasting, begin by comparing the 7-day and 9-day Mendoza itineraries.** Both include visits to specific wineries but differ in the language of the wine excursion, free time and whether Chile is included. For a family journey with varied interests, where some travelers want vineyards and others prefer glaciers and waterfalls, the longer route via El Calafate and Iguazu is worth exploring. For high-altitude wines and mountain landscapes, Cafayate is a better match.

This comparison does not replace the detailed tour itinerary. In each case, check which day the tasting is scheduled, which excursion is included and what requires an additional payment. The tour price by itself reveals neither the quality of the wines nor the number of tastings.

## When to travel and how to allocate your days

Argentina's seasons are the opposite of Europe's. In [Mendoza](/argentina/place/mendoza/), the grape harvest and related events generally occur toward the end of the Southern Hemisphere's summer; the national harvest festival usually takes place in March. Standard winery tours are not limited to harvest time, however: production visits, tastings and restaurant experiences are available in different seasons. Specific wineries receive visitors by reservation and according to their schedules.

For [Cafayate](/argentina/place/cafayate/), official tourism materials recommend, among other options, the period from April to November and an allowance of **2–4 days** to explore the region. This is guidance for the region itself, not a promised length of winery visits on every tour. On the five-day Amazing Salta trip, Cafayate appears at the beginning of the itinerary, and the following days are spent elsewhere in the northwest.

If combining the capital, Mendoza and Patagonia, allow time for domestic flights. A tasting after a long journey may be less enjoyable than a separate relaxed day among vineyards. For Cafayate, take overland travel from Salta into account. Do not assume that a tasting, winery lunch and additional excursion will automatically fit into one day without adjusting the program.

When choosing a trip, pay attention to four things:

- **What is actually included.** A winery tour, tasting, lunch and evening restaurant visit may be separate parts of the program.
- **Which excursions are optional.** For example, Luján de Cuyo is offered as an option for a free day on the 9-day wine tour.
- **How guiding is organized.** On one 7-day itinerary, the wine excursion is a group activity led by an English-speaking guide; a private format for the wider journey does not automatically change the format of every individual day.
- **Where the culinary day takes place.** On multi-country itineraries, it is particularly important not to confuse Argentine wineries with Chilean ones.

## Questions about food and wine tours in Argentina

### Which Ada Tours itineraries devote a substantial part of the program to tastings?

Primarily the [9-day wine itinerary](/multi-country/tour/chile-argentina-mendoza-wine-9-days/) and the [7-day food and wine journey](/argentina/tour/argentina-food-fine-living/). Both include a dedicated day visiting several Mendoza wineries. Longer sightseeing trips may include only one such day.

### Which should I choose, Mendoza or Cafayate?

Mendoza is best for comparing multiple wineries and Malbec; Cafayate for high-altitude Torrontés and combining wine with the mountains of the northwest. The published Ada Tours itineraries also differ in depth: one Uco Valley route schedules 3 estates, while Amazing Salta visits one winery and a wine museum.

### Is lunch included during a winery visit?

On the [9-day wine tour](/multi-country/tour/chile-argentina-mendoza-wine-9-days/), lunch at one winery is listed as part of the Uco Valley day. On the [El Calafate and Iguazu itinerary](/argentina/tour/argentina-buenos-aires-mendoza-el-calafate-iguazu/), lunch on the Uco Valley excursion is also included. On the [Amazing Salta tour](/argentina/tour/amazing-salta/), however, lunch in Cafayate's main square is paid separately. Check the conditions of your chosen route.

### Can I travel without taking part in alcoholic tastings?

Yes. Argentina also offers culinary experiences, gaucho culture and nature excursions. For example, the [Buenos Aires and Tigre group tour](/argentina/tour/argentina-experience-6-days/) includes asado, sightseeing and tango. However, whether an included paid tasting can be replaced with another activity depends on the conditions of the specific program, not on an automatic entitlement.

### Is there a culinary tour without wineries?

Yes. The [one-day king-crab excursion from Ushuaia](/argentina/tour/ushuaia-fishing/) focuses on fishing and local cuisine, without winery visits. For traditional grilled meat and pampas culture, consider gaucho outings near [Buenos Aires](/argentina/place/buenos-aires/).

### Can food and wine experiences be combined with Iguazu or Patagonia?

Yes. The [Mendoza, glaciers and Iguazu route](/argentina/tour/argentina-buenos-aires-mendoza-el-calafate-iguazu/) includes one wine day followed by other regions of the country. When choosing, count not just the tour's total days, but the time genuinely allocated to each region and culinary stop.
